notes:
Here are the verse-by-verse notes on Joel 2, from the sources I was able to access.

---

## JOEL 2 — VERSE-BY-VERSE NOTES

### v. 1
**"Blow the ram's horn in Zion; sound the alarm on My holy mountain!"**

Joel opens with an urgent call to the priests, whose duty it was to blow the trumpet (shofar) both for solemn assemblies and for warning of danger (Num. 10:3, 8). The trumpet here is to be blown with a "broken, quivering voice" (a tarantantara), signaling imminent danger. Zion, the temple mount, is called "My holy mountain," indicating God's special ownership even as judgment approaches.

— Gill (biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/joel/2.htm)
— Ellicott (biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/joel/2.htm)

**"For the Day of the LORD is coming; indeed, it is near."**

The "Day of the LORD" is the key theme. In Joel 1, the prophet described a locust plague that had already arrived; here in chapter 2, the "Day" is *near* — still future but imminent. Unlike the "day of the locusts" which was already present, what Joel now describes is a coming judgment. The Hebrew more literally reads "has come" — so certain that God sees it as already accomplished.

— Precept Austin (preceptaustin.org/joel-2-commentary)
— Enduring Word (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joel-2/)

**Interpretive debate:** Precept Austin notes four main approaches to Joel 2:1-11: (1) a plain literal locust invasion; (2) a figurative description using locust imagery to foreshadow a future military army; (3) a literal locust plague that functions typologically as a harbinger of the Day of the LORD; (4) a pure future military invasion with no locust referent. MacArthur, Wiersbe, Boice, Feinberg, and others favor view #2 — the locusts of Joel 1 are used as a "visual vocabulary" for a coming human army. Hubbard, Allen, and Keil & Delitzsch favor view #4 (literal-but-typological).

— Precept Austin (preceptaustin.org/joel-2-commentary)

---

### v. 2
**"A day of darkness and gloom, a day of clouds and blackness."**

This language evokes both the literal darkening caused by massive locust swarms (as in Exodus 10:15) and the figurative darkness of great calamity. Gill notes that locusts sometimes come in such numbers they "darken the heavens at noonday."

— Gill (biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/joel/2.htm)
— Matthew Henry (biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/joel/2.htm)

**"Like the dawn overspreading the mountains a great and strong army appears."**

Ellicott argues the Hebrew word for "morning" (shachar) here is better understood in its other sense of "blackness" — picturing a thick, dark, rolling cloud settled on the mountaintop. This fits the context of gloom better than "dawn." Either way, the image is of suddenness and inescapability: "as the morning light…diffuses itself in a moment."

— Ellicott (biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/joel/2.htm)
— Gill (biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/joel/2.htm)

**"Such as never was of old, nor will ever be in ages to come."**

Gill explains this hyperbolically refers to the uniqueness of the calamity *in the land of Judea* — not necessarily worldwide. He notes a rabbinic tradition that this refers to four kinds of locusts coming together, something unprecedented.

— Gill (biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/joel/2.htm)

---

### v. 3
**"Before them a fire devours, and behind them a flame scorches. The land before them is like the Garden of Eden, but behind them, it is like a desert wasteland."**

The locusts' consuming work is likened to fire: everything green is devoured; what remains behind is shriveled as if scorched. The contrast between Eden and desert captures total devastation. Nothing escapes. Gill adds that this also pictures the Assyrian or Chaldean armies who destroyed by fire and sword.

— Gill (biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/joel/2.htm)
— Ellicott (biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/joel/2.htm)

---

### vv. 4-5
**"Their appearance is like that of horses… like swift steeds… with a sound like that of chariots."**

The head of a locust resembles a horse's head (noted by Theodoret, Jerome, Bochart, and confirmed by Revelation 9:7). The comparison to "horsemen" and "chariots" emphasizes their swiftness and the terrifying noise. The rattling of chariots over rocky mountaintops and the crackling of fire consuming stubble both describe the overwhelming, inescapable din.

— Gill (biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/joel/2.htm)
— Ellicott (biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/joel/2.htm)
— Enduring Word (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joel-2/)

---

### v. 6
**"Nations writhe in horror before them; every face turns pale."**

Literally "all faces gather blackness" — the Hebrew phrase describes faces draining of color in terror. Ellicott notes alternative translations: some render it as faces becoming "like a pot" (blackened by fire). The same phrase appears in Nahum 2:10. The word "nations" (peoples) is one reason many interpreters see this as describing a human army rather than mere locusts.

— Ellicott (biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/joel/2.htm)
— Precept Austin (preceptaustin.org/joel-2-commentary)

---

### vv. 7-9
**"They charge like mighty men… each marches in formation, not swerving… they do not jostle one another… they burst through the defenses, never breaking ranks."**

Joel paints a picture of astonishing military discipline — no breaking of ranks, no pushing, each soldier in his own path. Jerome, writing from Palestine, testified that he witnessed locust swarms flying in such perfect order they "kept their place like checkered squares in a pavement" not deviating "a nail's breadth."

— Gill (biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/joel/2.htm)
— Enduring Word (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joel-2/)

**"They climb into houses, entering through windows like thieves."**

Locusts literally entered houses (Exodus 10:6; Pliny notes they "eat through even the doors"). Theodoret comments: "not only flying, but even creeping up the walls, they enter into houses at the windows." This also describes an invading army breaching the city.

— Gill (biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/joel/2.htm)
— Ellicott (biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/joel/2.htm)

**"When they fall upon the sword, they shall not be wounded" (v. 8, KJV).**

Gill notes this is explained variously: it may mean the locusts' small, smooth bodies are hard to cut with a sword; or that their sheer numbers make individual casualties irrelevant; or (following the Targum and Kimchi) that they "are not to be bribed" — unlike human soldiers, they cannot be bought off with money.

— Gill (biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/joel/2.htm)

---

### vv. 10-11
**"Before them the earth quakes; the heavens tremble. The sun and moon grow dark, and the stars lose their brightness."**

These cosmic signs go beyond mere locust imagery and point toward eschatological judgment. Some take the sun, moon, and stars figuratively for kings, nobles, and common people thrown into consternation; others see it as literal cosmic disturbances accompanying the Day of the LORD, paralleling Jesus' words in Matthew 24:29 and Revelation 6:12-17.

— Ellicott (biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/joel/2.htm)
— Gill (biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/joel/2.htm)

**"The LORD raises His voice in the presence of His army… For the Day of the LORD is great and very dreadful. Who can endure it?"**

Crucially, the army — whether locusts or human invaders — is *God's* army. "His camp is very large." He is the General at the head, uttering His voice to command them. The question "Who can endure it?" (cf. Mal. 3:2; Rev. 6:17) is left unanswered, paving the way for the call to repentance that follows. The "Day of the LORD" bookends this section (vv. 1 and 11).

— Enduring Word (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joel-2/)
— Precept Austin (preceptaustin.org/joel-2-commentary)
— Gill (biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/joel/2.htm)

---

### v. 12
**"'Yet even now,' declares the LORD, 'return to Me with all your heart, with fasting, weeping, and mourning.'"**

The word "declares" (Hebrew *ne'um*) is an especially weighty, authoritative divine utterance — the same word used in Psalm 110:1 ("The LORD said to my Lord"). God does not merely threaten; He invites. Even with judgment at the doorstep, true repentance is never too late. The call is to sincerity: "with all your heart," expressed outwardly through fasting, weeping, and mourning — but only as genuine expressions, not mere externals.

— Ellicott (biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/joel/2.htm)
— Enduring Word (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joel-2/)
— Matthew Henry (biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/joel/2.htm)

---

### v. 13
**"Rend your hearts and not your garments."**

Tearing garments was the customary Jewish expression of grief. Joel does not absolutely forbid it, but insists that without heart-rending, the outward sign is a mockery. Matthew Henry: "The sign without the thing signified is but a jest…and an affront to God." Enduring Word recounts Spurgeon's story of a woman who made a show of repentance but, when tested against the Ten Commandments, could not find a single one she had broken — her repentance was fake.

— Matthew Henry (biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/joel/2.htm)
— Enduring Word (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joel-2/)
— Gill (biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/joel/2.htm)

**"For He is gracious and compassionate, slow to anger, abounding in loving devotion. And He relents from sending disaster."**

This is one of the classic Old Testament creedal statements about God's character, echoing Exodus 34:6-7. The motivation for repentance is not terror alone but confidence in God's mercy. Enduring Word notes: "Ultimately, it is His goodness that leads us to repentance (Romans 2:4)."

— Enduring Word (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joel-2/)
— Gill (biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/joel/2.htm)

---

### v. 14
**"Who knows? He may turn and relent and leave a blessing behind Him."**

The "who knows?" expresses humble hope, not doubt about God's character. It recognizes that God is sovereignly free — repentance does not obligate Him, but His revealed character gives strong grounds for hope. The blessing named is the restoration of grain and drink offerings, which had ceased due to the devastation (Joel 1:9, 13).

— Ellicott (biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/joel/2.htm)
— Enduring Word (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joel-2/)

---

### vv. 15-16
**"Blow the ram's horn in Zion, consecrate a fast, proclaim a sacred assembly. Gather the people…"**

Now the trumpet is blown not for alarm (as in v. 1) but to call a solemn assembly of repentance. No one is exempt: elders, children, even nursing infants, the bridegroom from his chamber, the bride from her dressing room. Normally a newly married man was exempt even from military service (Deut. 24:5), but here the crisis is so grave that even the wedding chamber must be vacated. True repentance does not carry on with "business as usual."

— Ellicott (biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/joel/2.htm)
— Enduring Word (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joel-2/)
— Matthew Henry (biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/joel/2.htm)

---

### v. 17
**"Let the priests who minister before the LORD weep between the portico and the altar…"**

The priests are to stand in the space between the temple porch and the altar of burnt offering — a public, visible place of intercession. Their prayer appeals to God's honor: "Spare Your people… do not make Your heritage a reproach… Why should they say among the peoples, 'Where is their God?'" The argument is that judgment on Israel would cause the nations to question God's power or faithfulness. All mention of locusts is now dropped; the focus is entirely on the threat of foreign domination.

— Ellicott (biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/joel/2.htm)
— Enduring Word (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joel-2/)

---

### v. 18
**"Then the LORD became jealous for His land, and He spared His people."**

This is the great turning point of the book. The Hebrew construction signals a dramatic shift: God's jealousy (zeal) for His land is aroused, and He pities His people. The assumption is that the repentance called for in vv. 12-17 has occurred. God's response is not reluctant but zealous.

— Enduring Word (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joel-2/)
— Precept Austin (preceptaustin.org/joel-2-commentary)

---

### vv. 19-20
**"I will send you grain, new wine, and oil… The northern army I will drive away from you."**

God promises material restoration and military deliverance. "The northern army" (literally "him of the north") is significant: Ellicott notes the Hebrew includes a patronymic suffix indicating a *native* of the north, which excludes a reference to mere locusts. Invading armies (Assyrian, Babylonian) typically came from the north (Jer. 1:13-14). The army's front ranks are driven into the "Eastern Sea" (Dead Sea) and its rear guard into the "Western Sea" (Mediterranean), with their corpses producing a foul stench — recalling the plague of locusts in Egypt being cast into the Red Sea (Ex. 10:19).

— Ellicott (biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/joel/2.htm)
— Enduring Word (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joel-2/)

---

### vv. 21-22
**"Do not be afraid, O land; rejoice and be glad… Do not be afraid, O beasts of the field…"**

The whole created order — land, beasts, and people — is summoned to rejoice. The pastures turn green, trees bear fruit, fig tree and vine yield their best. Joel speaks with the "eye of faith," seeing restoration as already accomplished. God's great works are the ground of confidence.

— Enduring Word (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joel-2/)
— Ellicott (biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/joel/2.htm)

---

### v. 23
**"He has given you the autumn rains for your vindication… both autumn and spring rains, as before."**

"Former rain" (autumn, October-November) and "latter rain" (spring, March-April) were essential for agriculture in rain-dependent Israel. The marginal/Vulgate reading "teacher of righteousness" (from the Hebrew *moreh*) led some to see a messianic reference here, though most Protestant commentators take it as referring to rain. Ellicott's preferred reading is "as before" for "in the first month."

**Denominational note on "Latter Rain":** The phrase "former and latter rain" became the namesake of the Latter Rain movement (begun 1948 by William Branham), which taught that a "new Pentecost" with restored sign-gifts would come at the end of the age. Enduring Word notes this movement "popularized many attitudes and doctrines prominent in some revival movements today," including the five-fold ministry, replacement theology, and dominion theology. Gaebelein (dispensational) strongly rejects any spiritualized reading of "early and latter rain," calling such teaching "extremely fanciful" and noting that nowhere does the New Testament promise a "latter rain" outpouring; rather, the age ends in apostasy (2 Thess. 2:3-17). (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/gab/joel-2.html)

— Enduring Word (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joel-2/)
— Ellicott (biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/joel/2.htm)

---

### v. 24
**"The threshing floors will be full of grain, and the vats will overflow with new wine and oil."**

A picture of overflowing abundance — the precise reversal of the devastation in Joel 1. Full threshing floors and overflowing vats signal that God's blessing has returned in tangible, material form.

— Enduring Word (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joel-2/)

---

### v. 25
**"I will repay you for the years eaten by locusts… My great army that I sent against you."**

God identifies the locusts as "My great army" — they were His instruments of chastisement. Four Hebrew terms for locust are listed (swarming, young, destroying, devouring), corresponding to the four kinds in Joel 1:4. The promise to "repay the years" is striking: time itself cannot be recovered, but God can restore "the fruits of those years" — the harvests, the lost productivity, the wasted blessings. Spurgeon is quoted: "You cannot have back your time; but there is a strange and wonderful way in which God can give back to you the wasted blessings."

**Use in prosperity teaching:** This verse is often cited in Word of Faith and prosperity gospel circles as a promise that God will supernaturally restore lost finances, years, and opportunities. Traditional commentators apply it to God's covenant restoration of Israel's agricultural and national life, not as a blanket promise of wealth to individual believers.

— Enduring Word (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joel-2/)

---

### vv. 26-27
**"You will have plenty to eat… You will praise the name of the LORD your God, who has worked wonders for you. My people will never again be put to shame."**

The restoration leads to satisfaction, praise, and the removal of shame. The twice-repeated "never again be put to shame" emphasizes the finality of God's deliverance. Verse 27 gives the ultimate purpose: "Then you will know that I am present in Israel and that I am the LORD your God, and there is no other."

— Enduring Word (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joel-2/)
— Ellicott (biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/joel/2.htm)

---

### vv. 28-29
**"And afterward, I will pour out My Spirit on all people. Your sons and daughters will prophesy, your old men will dream dreams, your young men will see visions."**

This is one of the most debated passages in Joel. The key questions are: Was this fulfilled at Pentecost, or is it still future?

**View 1 — Fulfilled at Pentecost (classic Reformed, many evangelicals):** Peter explicitly quotes this passage in Acts 2:16-21, saying "this is that which was spoken by the prophet Joel." Under the old covenant, the Spirit came upon select individuals (kings, prophets, priests) for specific tasks. Joel foretells a new covenant reality in which the Spirit is poured out on "all flesh" — sons and daughters, old and young, even menservants and maidservants. Enduring Word argues this was fulfilled when the 120 disciples — common folk, not special office-holders — were filled with the Spirit at Pentecost. Ligonier's devotional "A Better Age" states: "On Pentecost, Peter explicitly identified the era in which he lived as the 'last days'… We are now living in the eschatological age of the Spirit" — and rejects the idea that a distinct "latter rain" outpouring is yet to come. (learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/better-age)

— Enduring Word (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joel-2/)
— Ellicott (biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/joel/2.htm)

**View 2 — Partial fulfillment / inaugurated but not consummated:** Many scholars (including NET Bible notes) argue that Pentecost was an *incipient* fulfillment — the messianic age had begun, but Joel's prophecy was not exhaustively fulfilled. The cosmic signs of vv. 30-31 had no counterpart at Pentecost. Peter's "this is that" uses a pesher-type formula (similar to Qumran) that identifies the event as relevant to the prophecy without claiming exhaustive fulfillment. A yet-future fulfillment associated with Christ's return remains. (classic.net.bible.org/passage.php?passage=joe+2%3A28-32)

— Precept Austin (preceptaustin.org/joel-2-commentary)

**View 3 — Entirely future (dispensational):** Gaebelein argues that Peter did *not* use the word "fulfilled"; he said "this is that" (Acts 2:16), drawing an analogy, not claiming fulfillment. He contends Joel's prophecy is for Israel in the future day of the Lord and has no application to the present church age. The Holy Spirit came at Pentecost for "a special purpose, which was the formation of the Church," but the full Joel prophecy awaits Christ's return and Israel's national restoration. (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/gab/joel-2.html)

**Pentecostal view:** Pentecostals generally see Acts 2 as the *beginning* of Joel's fulfillment — the "early rain" — and anticipate a "latter rain" outpouring at the end of the age with restored charismatic gifts. Some associated the Azusa Street revival (1906) and subsequent Pentecostal movements with this expected latter rain. This view is contested by Reformed cessationists (Ligonier) and dispensationalists (Gaebelein) alike.

---

### vv. 30-31
**"I will show wonders in the heavens and on the earth, blood and fire and columns of smoke. The sun will be turned to darkness and the moon to blood before the coming of the great and awesome Day of the LORD."**

These cosmic signs recall the plagues of Egypt and are taken up by Jesus in the Olivet Discourse (Matt. 24:29) and by John in Revelation 6:12 ("the sixth seal"). The language is apocalyptic and points to the final Day of the LORD. Ellicott notes these signs may include "the luminaries in heaven and the potentates on earth." The "great and awesome Day" echoes v. 11.

— Ellicott (biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/joel/2.htm)
— Matthew Henry (biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/joel/2.htm)

---

### v. 32
**"And everyone who calls on the name of the LORD will be saved; for on Mount Zion and in Jerusalem there will be deliverance, as the LORD has promised, among the remnant called by the LORD."**

This is one of the great salvation promises of the Old Testament. Paul quotes it in Romans 10:13 to prove the universality of gospel salvation — Jew and Gentile alike. The "remnant" theme is central: salvation is not automatic for ethnic Israel but for those whom "the LORD calls."

**Reformed reading:** The emphasis on "the remnant whom the LORD calls" aligns with the Reformed doctrine of effectual calling — salvation belongs to those God sovereignly calls.

**Baptist/Evangelical reading:** The promise "whoever calls…shall be saved" is "broad, personal, and certain" (Enduring Word, citing Spurgeon: "we cannot shut ourselves out of 'whosoever'"). It emphasizes human responsibility to call upon the Lord, paired with divine sovereignty in calling.

**Catholic/Orthodox reading:** The deliverance "in Mount Zion and in Jerusalem" is understood typologically as the Church, the heavenly Jerusalem, where salvation is found (Ellicott references this). (biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/joel/2.htm)

**Lutheran note:** Lutherans would emphasize that this promise is pure gospel — salvation by grace through faith, not by works — and that "calling on the name of the LORD" is itself a work of the Spirit.

— Enduring Word (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joel-2/)
— Ellicott (biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/joel/2.htm)

---

## SUMMARY OF TRADITIONAL DIFFERENCES ON KEY POINTS

| Issue | View | Sources |
|-------|------|---------|
| **Joel 2:1-11 — Locusts or army?** | Literal locusts only (some scholars); Locust imagery foreshadowing human army (MacArthur, Boice, Wiersbe, Feinberg); Locusts as typological harbinger (Hubbard, Allen, Keil) | preceptaustin.org/joel-2-commentary |
| **vv. 28-32 — Fulfilled or future?** | Fulfilled at Pentecost (Reformed, many evangelicals); Partially fulfilled with future completion (NET Bible, many scholars); Entirely future for Israel (dispensational/Gaebelein) | enduringword.com; studylight.org/commentaries/eng/gab/joel-2.html; classic.net.bible.org |
| **"Latter Rain" (v. 23)** | Means literal spring rain (most traditional); Misapplied to a second Pentecost outpouring (Latter Rain movement, some Pentecostals) | enduringword.com; studylight.org/commentaries/eng/gab/joel-2.html |
| **v. 25 "Restore the years"** | Covenant restoration of agricultural prosperity (traditional); Used by prosperity gospel to promise supernatural financial recovery | enduringword.com |
| **v. 32 "Whoever calls"** | Emphasizes human responsibility (Baptist/evangelical, Spurgeon); Emphasizes divine calling of the remnant (Reformed); Typological fulfillment in the Church (Catholic/Orthodox) | enduringword.com; biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/joel/2.htm |
